rows.stem: The molar ionic conductivities of \(\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}\) and \(\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}\) are 106.0 \(\mathrm{S\ cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\) and 160.0 \(\mathrm{S\ cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\) respectively. The value of limiting molar conductivity of \(\mathrm{MgSO_4}\) will be :
rows.solution:
By Kohlrausch's law the limiting molar conductivity is the sum of the contributions of ALL the ions the formula unit gives, each counted as often as it appears.

Magnesium sulphate gives ONE magnesium ion and ONE sulphate ion, so each contribution is counted once:
\(\Lambda_m^{\circ}(\mathrm{MgSO_4}) = \lambda^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}} + \lambda^{\circ}_{\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}}\)
\(= 106{\cdot}0 + 160{\cdot}0\)

\(\Lambda_m^{\circ} = 266\ \mathrm{S\ cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\)

Note that the CHARGES do not enter the arithmetic — only the NUMBER of each ion in the formula does. A doubly charged ion has a large ionic conductivity of its own, and that is already built into the figure supplied.

The contrast is calcium chloride, \(\mathrm{CaCl_2}\), where the chloride contribution must be counted TWICE. Here the 1:1 stoichiometry means a plain sum.

rows.stem: In effective collisions the colliding molecules must have :

options.label: B
options.text: A certain minimum amount of activation energy.

options.label: D
options.text: Threshold energy and proper orientation both.

rows.solution:
An effective collision requires THRESHOLD ENERGY AND PROPER ORIENTATION BOTH.

Most collisions lead to no reaction at all, and they fail on one of two counts.

ENERGY. The colliding molecules must carry at least the threshold energy — the sum of their average energy and the activation energy — or the existing bonds cannot be broken. The fraction that do is \(e^{-E_a/RT}\), which is why heating speeds a reaction up so sharply.

ORIENTATION. Even an energetic collision fails if the molecules meet the wrong way round: the atoms that are to bond must be brought together, not the far ends of the molecules. That requirement is what the pre-exponential factor \(A\) in the Arrhenius equation accounts for.

Both conditions must hold at once, which is why the options naming only one of them are incomplete.

rows.stem: Identify the secondary amine from the given options :
rows.solution:
The secondary amine is \(\mathrm{CH_3NHCH(CH_3)_2}\).

An amine is classified by how many CARBON GROUPS are attached to its NITROGEN — not by the kind of carbon the nitrogen sits on, which is the distinction this question is testing.

Here the nitrogen carries a methyl group on one side and an isopropyl group on the other, with one hydrogen remaining. Two carbon groups on nitrogen makes it SECONDARY.

The other three are all PRIMARY: each has a single carbon attached to the nitrogen, and two hydrogens. That remains true of \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_2CHNH_2}\) and \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_3CNH_2}\) even though the carbons carrying the nitrogen are themselves secondary and tertiary.

The classification of an ALCOHOL works the other way round, by the carbon bearing the hydroxyl, which is where the confusion comes from.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Bromination of Phenol can be carried out even in the absence of Lewis acid.
Reason (R) : \(\mathrm{-OH}\) group of Phenol has the high activation effect.
rows.context: For questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given – one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
Both statements are true and the Reason IS the correct explanation of the Assertion.

Bromination of phenol needs no Lewis acid, and the Reason gives the cause exactly.

Bromination of BENZENE requires a catalyst such as iron(III) bromide, whose job is to polarise the bromine molecule into a strong enough electrophile for an ordinary ring to attack. Phenol's ring does not need that help.

The hydroxyl group is strongly ACTIVATING: its lone pair is delocalised into the ring by resonance, raising the electron density markedly at the ortho and para positions. The ring is then reactive enough to attack even the feeble electrophile present in bromine itself.

In WATER the activation is greater still, because phenol ionises to phenoxide, and all three positions are substituted at once to give 2,4,6-tribromophenol as a white precipitate.

rows.subtopic: Factors Influencing Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem:
Define the following terms :
(a) Molecularity of reaction
(b) Complex reaction
rows.solution:
(a) MOLECULARITY of a reaction is the number of reacting species — atoms, ions or molecules — that must COLLIDE SIMULTANEOUSLY in an ELEMENTARY reaction for it to occur.

It is a THEORETICAL quantity, read off the proposed mechanism rather than measured, and being a count of colliding species it must be a WHOLE NUMBER and at least 1. It is defined only for an elementary reaction.

(b) A COMPLEX REACTION is one that occurs through a SERIES OF STEPS rather than in a single step — a sequence of elementary reactions, each with its own molecularity.

Two consequences follow. Such a reaction has NO single molecularity to quote, since the steps may differ. And its observed ORDER is set by the SLOWEST step, the rate determining one, which is why order must be measured and may turn out to be zero or fractional.

rows.subtopic: Colligative Properties and Determination of Molar Mass
rows.stem: Calculate the molar mass of a compound when 6.3 g of it is dissolved in 27 g of chloroform to form a solution that has a boiling point of \(68.04\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\). The boiling point of pure chloroform is \(61.04\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) and \(\mathrm{K_b}\) for chloroform is \(3.63\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C\ kg\ mol^{-1}}\).
rows.solution:
The solution boils at \(68{\cdot}04\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) and pure chloroform at \(61{\cdot}04\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\), so the elevation is
\(\Delta T_b = 68{\cdot}04 - 61{\cdot}04 = 7\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\)

Combine the boiling point elevation formula with the mass data:
\(\Delta T_b = \dfrac{K_b \times w_B \times 1000}{M_B \times w_A}\)

Rearranging for the molar mass, with \(w_B = 6{\cdot}3\) g of solute and \(w_A = 27\) g of chloroform:
\(M_B = \dfrac{K_b \times w_B \times 1000}{\Delta T_b \times w_A} = \dfrac{3{\cdot}63 \times 6{\cdot}3 \times 1000}{7 \times 27}\)
\(= \dfrac{22869}{189}\)

\(M_B = 121\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\)

Note that the temperatures may be used in degrees Celsius here, because only their DIFFERENCE enters and a difference is the same on either scale. The absolute values would matter only if a temperature appeared on its own.

rows.stem:
Which of the following compounds will react more rapidly by \(\mathrm{S_N2}\) reaction & why ?
(a) \(\mathrm{CH_3-C(CH_3)_2-Br}\) or \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-CH(Br)-CH_3}\)
(b) Arrange the following compounds in the increasing order of their boiling points :
\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2CH_2Br}\), \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_2CH-CH_2Br}\), \(\mathrm{CH_3-C(CH_3)(Br)-CH_3}\)
rows.solution:
(a) \(\mathrm{CH_3{-}CH_2{-}CH(Br){-}CH_3}\), 2-bromobutane, reacts more rapidly.

An \(\mathrm{S_N}2\) reaction requires the nucleophile to attack the carbon from the side directly OPPOSITE the leaving group, so the rate is governed by how ACCESSIBLE that carbon is.

2-Bromobutane is a SECONDARY halide: the carbon carrying the bromine has one hydrogen and two alkyl groups. \((\mathrm{CH_3})_3\mathrm{C{-}Br}\) is TERTIARY — three alkyl groups surround its carbon and block the approach from behind almost completely.

Steric hindrance, not electronics, is what decides, and the order runs primary, secondary, tertiary with tertiary halides essentially unreactive by this route. Note that the \(\mathrm{S_N}1\) order runs exactly the opposite way.

(b) Increasing order of boiling point:
\((\mathrm{CH_3})_3\mathrm{C{-}Br} < (\mathrm{CH_3})_2\mathrm{CH{-}CH_2Br} < \mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2CH_2Br}\)

All three are isomers with the same molecular mass, so the difference lies in SHAPE. Boiling point depends on van der Waals forces, and those depend on how much surface two molecules can present to each other.

The more BRANCHED an isomer, the more nearly spherical it is, the smaller its surface area, and the weaker the forces between its molecules. The tertiary bromide is the most branched and boils lowest; the straight chain is the least branched and boils highest.

rows.stem:
(a) What happens when Glucose reacts with HI ? Write chemical equation.
(b) Which type of bond holds a DNA double helix together ?
rows.solution:
(a) WITH HYDROGEN IODIDE and red phosphorus on prolonged heating, glucose is reduced all the way to N-HEXANE:
\(\mathrm{CHO(CHOH)_4CH_2OH} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{HI}} \mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2CH_2CH_2CH_3}\)

Every oxygen is stripped out, and the product is a STRAIGHT chain of six carbons. That result is one of the classic proofs of glucose's structure: it shows the six carbons are joined in an UNBRANCHED chain, since a branched skeleton would have given a branched hexane.

(b) HYDROGEN BONDS hold the two strands of a DNA double helix together.

They form between specific pairs of bases — adenine with thymine through TWO such bonds, guanine with cytosine through THREE. That specificity is what makes the two strands complementary rather than identical, and it is what allows each strand to serve as the template for the other during replication.

The bonds are individually weak, which is what lets the helix be unwound when the information is needed, but there are so many of them along the molecule that the double helix is stable.

rows.stem:
(a) Draw the geometrical isomers of the given complex :
\(\mathrm{[Co(en)_2Cl_2]^{+}}\)
(b) Write the electronic configuration of \(\mathrm{d^4}\) ion if \(\Delta_0 > \mathrm{P}\).
(c) What is a didentate ligand ? Give one example.
rows.solution:
(a) \(\mathrm{[Co(en)_2Cl_2]^{+}}\) is octahedral with two chlorido ligands and two bidentate diamines, so the two chlorides may sit adjacent or opposite.

CIS ISOMER: the two chlorido ligands on ADJACENT positions, with the two diamine ligands spanning the remaining four. This form has no plane of symmetry and is therefore also optically active, existing as a pair of enantiomers.

TRANS ISOMER: the two chlorido ligands directly OPPOSITE each other along one axis, with the two chelate rings lying in the plane between them. This form has a plane of symmetry and is optically inactive.

(b) \(\Delta_{\mathrm{o}} > \mathrm{P}\) means the splitting costs MORE than pairing, so electrons fill the lower set completely before any goes up. For \(d^4\):
\(t_{2g}^4\,e_g^0\)
with two unpaired electrons — a LOW SPIN complex. Had \(\Delta_{\mathrm{o}}\) been the smaller, the configuration would have been \(t_{2g}^3\,e_g^1\), high spin, with four.

(c) A DIDENTATE ligand is one that binds the metal through TWO DONOR ATOMS AT THE SAME TIME, closing a ring that includes the metal — a CHELATE ring.

Example: ethane-1,2-diamine, which binds through both of its nitrogens; the oxalate ion, \(\mathrm{C_2O_4^{2-}}\), which binds through two of its oxygens, serves equally well.

Chelation gives such complexes extra stability, an effect large enough to have its own name. Note that didentate is not the same as AMBIDENTATE: a didentate ligand uses two atoms at once, while an ambidentate one merely has a choice of two.

rows.stem:
Define the following terms :
(a) Non essential amino acids.
(b) Monosaccharides
(c) Anomers
rows.solution:
(a) NON-ESSENTIAL AMINO ACIDS are those the body CAN synthesise for itself, so they need not be supplied in the diet. Glycine and alanine are examples.

The contrast is with ESSENTIAL amino acids, such as valine, leucine and lysine, which the body cannot make and which must come from food. The name describes what the DIET must supply, not how important the acid is — both kinds are needed for protein synthesis.

(b) MONOSACCHARIDES are carbohydrates that CANNOT BE HYDROLYSED FURTHER into simpler carbohydrates. Each is a single polyhydroxy aldehyde or ketone — glucose, fructose, ribose.

They are the units from which the larger carbohydrates are built: a disaccharide hydrolyses to two of them, a polysaccharide to many.

(c) ANOMERS are a pair of cyclic sugars that differ ONLY in the configuration of the hydroxyl group at the ANOMERIC CARBON — \(\mathrm{C_1}\) in an aldose such as glucose, \(\mathrm{C_2}\) in a ketose such as fructose.

That carbon becomes a new stereocentre when the ring closes, and its hydroxyl can end up on either side: BELOW the plane in the \(\alpha\) form, ABOVE it in the \(\beta\) form. Everything else about the two molecules is identical.

In solution the two interconvert through the open-chain form, which is what MUTAROTATION is.

rows.stem:
(a) Write the IUPAC name of the given compound :
(b) Why are haloalkanes more reactive towards nucleophilic substitution reactions than haloarenes ?
(c) What happens when ethyl chloride is treated with aqueous KOH ?
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — part (a) prints a DRAWN structure and asks for its IUPAC name, so the figure IS the question: a six-membered ring drawn as a hexagon with three inner double-bond lines (a Kekule ring, verified at 4x — it is not a plain hexagon), carrying a two-letter halogen label on one vertex and a different one-letter halogen label on the vertex directly opposite. It is deliberately NOT named or given as a formula, because naming it would state the answer; the official marking scheme's own answer confirms the ring is benzene. Page idx 14.
rows.solution:
(a) The compound is a benzene ring carrying a bromine and a chlorine on opposite carbons.

Substituents are cited alphabetically, bromo before chloro, and the ring is numbered to give the lowest locants:
1-BROMO-4-CHLOROBENZENE

The para arrangement could equally be written as p-bromochlorobenzene, but the numbered form is the systematic one.

(b) Because in a HALOARENE the carbon-halogen bond is much harder to break, for two reasons that reinforce each other.

The halogen's lone pair is delocalised INTO THE RING by resonance, so the \(\mathrm{C-X}\) bond acquires partial DOUBLE BOND character: it is shorter and stronger, and a bond with double bond character does not break to let a nucleophile substitute.

And the carbon carrying the halogen is \(sp^2\) hybridised rather than \(sp^3\). An \(sp^2\) carbon has more s character, is more electronegative, and holds the shared pair more tightly.

Two further factors point the same way: the ring's electron-rich \(\pi\) cloud REPELS an approaching nucleophile, and the phenyl cation that a unimolecular route would require is extremely unstable.

A haloalkane has none of these obstacles — its carbon is \(sp^3\), its bond is a plain single bond, and its carbocation is comparatively stable.

(c) SUBSTITUTION occurs and ETHANOL is formed.

Aqueous potassium hydroxide supplies the HYDROXIDE ion, which is a good NUCLEOPHILE in water. It attacks the carbon bearing the chlorine and substitutes for it:
\(\mathrm{C_2H_5Cl} + \mathrm{KOH(aq)} \longrightarrow \mathrm{C_2H_5OH} + \mathrm{KCl}\)

ALCOHOLIC potassium hydroxide would have given ETHENE instead: there the reagent supplies ALKOXIDE ions, which are much stronger bases but bulkier and poorer nucleophiles, so they attack a \(\beta\) hydrogen and eliminate rather than substitute.

Substitution and elimination are always in competition; what the solvent changes is which one wins.
